full_judgment:
Mr. Md. Imman Ali, J.:- This is an application filed under Article 102(1) and (2)(a)(i) of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh. 

2. The petitioners are learned advocates of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh and filed the instant application as a Public Interest Litigation (PIL) with the view to uphold the "Supremacy of the Constitution" and "Rule of Law for ensuring independence of the judiciary from other organs of the State. They are concerned about the deviations made by the government on four occasions in the recent past from the recognised well established Constitutional Convention to appoint the senior-most judge of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh as the Chief Justice of Bangladesh. It is stated in the petition that it is a fundamental right of every Citizen to have access to impartial and independent Courts/Tribunals and the exercise of that right is dependent on the independence of judiciary which can be secured only through appointment of persons of high integrity, repute and competence, strictly in accordance with the procedure prescribed under the Constitution, to the high office of Judges of superior Court. The selection of a person to the high office of the Chief Justice of Bangladesh in a pivotal appointment for maintaining the independence of the judiciary and for providing a free and unobstructed access to impartial and independent Courts/Tribunals to the ordinary citizens. Any deviation from the method prescribed under Constitution for appointment to the high office of Chief Justice of Bangladesh would give rise to infringement of the right of a citizen to have free, fair and equal access to independent and impartial Courts/Tribunals. It is further contended that if the appointments of Judges are not made in the manner prescribed in the constitution then the same will be detrimental to the independence of the judiciary which will lead to lack of confidence among the people. 

3. Mr. Hassan M.S. Azim, Learned advocate appearing in person as petitioner No. 1 submits that the Rule of seniority, i.e. the senior-most Judge of the Supreme Court to be appointed as the Chief Justice of Bangladesh is an established convention and the same exists in India and Pakistan. By reference to the decisions of the Indian Supreme Court in the case of Supreme Court Advocates-on Record Association and another v. Union of India with S.P. Gupta. V. Union of India, AIR 1994 Supreme Court 264 and the cases of Malik Asad Ali and others versus Federation of Pakistan through Secretary, Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs, Islamabad and other, PLD 1998 Supreme Court 161 and in the case of Al-Jehad Trust through Raeesul Mujahideen Habib-ul-Wahabb-ul-khairi and others versus Federation of Pakistan and others, P LD 1996 Supreme Court 324, he submits that the Supreme Court of India and Pakistan have upheld the Constitutional Convention that the senior-most Judge of the Supreme Court would be appointed as Chief Justice of India and Pakistan respectively. He further submits that the appointment of the senior-most Judge leads to certainty in the process of appointment and avoids any bias for ulterior motives or extraneous reasons. He also submits that the system of appointing the Chief Justice from the senior-most Judge leads to an independent judiciary inasmuch as the Judges will work towards achieving the ultimate goal of reaching the pinnacle and will work without any fear or favour. He points out from the decision in the Al-Jehad case that if the system of appointing the senior-most judge in not adhered to then those who are not so senior will strive to please the party in power in order to be appointed the Chief Justice in supersession of their senior colleagues. Echoing the dictum of his Lordship Manzoor Hussain Sial, J. he submits that the senior-most Judge entertains a legitimate expectancy to be considered for appointment as Chief Justice. 

4. Mr. Azim further submits that our Constitution itself indicates in Article 97 that the senior-most Judge of the Supreme Court is given priority in the absence of the Chief Justice from his office. He further submits that this Article is indicative of the fact that the senior-most Judge of the Supreme Court is accepted as the most appropriate person to take the place of the Chief Justice. He submits that supersession of the senior Judges of the Supreme Court in appointing the Chief Justice undermines morale of the Judges of the Supreme Court and as such also the Rule of Law. He points out that in the past, where supersession has taken piece in this country, political motives have always played a big role and as a result the independence of the judiciary has been adversely affected. He submits that, therefore, certainty in the process and for the sake of transparency the system of appointing the senior-most Judge of the Supreme Court as the Chief Justice of the county should be adhered to. He further submits that should there arise any particular reason for not appointing the senior-most Judge as the Chief Justice of the country, then there must be reasons given and those reasons must be apparent and must be notified in the official gazette. The learned advocate points out that apart from the few recent occasions of Suppression, there has always been conformity with the age-old convention of appointing the senior-most Judge of the Supreme Court as the Chief Justice of Bangladesh. By reference to supersession of Mr. Justice Md. Ruhul Amin and Mr. Justice Mohammad Fazlul Karim and the subsequent appointment of both of them as Chief Justice shows that there could not have been any valid reason for not appointing them to the position of Chief Justice at the first instance since it could not be said that they were lacking in merit. He submits that the failure to appoint Mr. Justice Md. Ruhul Amin and Mr. Justice Mohammad Fazlul Karim in their turn as the senior-most Judge of the Supreme Court and their subsequent appointments as Chief Justice indicates that their super session initially was an arbitrary exercise of power by the appointing authority. 

5. In view of the importance of the matter Mr. Mahbubey Alam, learned Attorney General appeared and made submissions opposing the petition. 

6. The learned Attorney General submitted that there is no such rule as a rule of seniority and the suggestion by the petitioners that the reasons for not appointing the senior-most Judge as Chief Justice must be published in the official gazette is not an acceptable proposition, since that would expose the Hon'ble Judges of the Supreme Court, who are superseded, to ridicule. On the other hand, he submitted that the appointment of the Chief Justice of any country should be based on merit. He pointed out that the position of Chief Justice is not simply to provide the service of a judicial officer, but also involves many other administrative functions for which expertise is necessary and those matters are required to be considered when appointing the Chief Justice of the country. He pointed out from the provisions of the Constitution that there is no mandate for the appointment of the Chief Justice to be made from the senior- most Judge of the Supreme Court. He further pointed out that there is no constitutional convention to appoint on the basis of the seniority. By way of explanation he pointed out that all Judges of the Supreme Court, once appointed, carry the same weight and the judgments pronounced by them also carries equal weight. There is no question of any Judge being junior or less important than any other who is senior. Each Judge, including those who are not yet confirmed, i.e. within the two year period as Additional Judge, have the same power of pronouncing judgment and have the power also to deliver a dissenting judgment. Equally, the judgment of any puisne Judge is equal to the judgment of the Chief Justice of this country. This status and tenure of all Judges of the Supreme Court including that of the Chief Justice are the sole and each of them will retire upon reaching the age of 67 years and none can be removed other than by way of reference to the supreme Judicial Council.

 7. The learned Attorney General further pointed out that any appointment on the basis of seniority alone would detract from the efficiency in the judiciary, particularly if any Judge is of the view that he will reach the top no matter what his merit and acumen might be. The knowledge of his automatic accession would not enhance his performance, whereas if the appointment is made on the basis of merit, then the Judges will work towards achieving better efficiency in order to reach the top. He submitted that criteria should be based on order to reach the top. He submitted that the criteria should be based on merit at the first instance and then, amongst equally meritorious candidates, the senior-most would be taken. The selection on the basis of merit will give rise to intellectual competition which should be kept alive for the betterment of the judiciary. Referring to the Constitution, the learned Attorney General pointed out that the appointment of the Chief Justice is solely the prerogative of the President. By way of contrast, he pointed out that Article 48(3) of the Constitution requires that the President take advice from the Prime Minister in the case of appointment of Judges of the Supreme Court other than the Chief Justice. In the case of the appointment of the Chief Justice, the prerogative lies alone with the President. He further pointed out that it is entirely up to the President whom he will consult with regard to the appointment in order to find out who among the Judges of the Supreme Court is capable of doing the administrative as well as the judicial functions of the Chief Justice. The learned Attorney General further pointed out that the reference by the petitioner to a Constitutional Convention is not established; since admittedly the convention has been broken on 4/5 occasions and none challenged the breach of the convention of appointing from the senior-most Judge of the Supreme Court. He submitted, therefore, that the present petition was not filed bona fide. 

8. With regard to the submissions of the petitioner that Article 97 indicates that the senior-most Judge of the Supreme Court is fit to take the place of the Chief Justice, the learned Attorney General pointed out that the same Article of the Constitution refers to the performing of the function by the senior-most Judge in the place of Chief Justice until some other person has entered upon that office. He submits, therefore, that precisely excludes the concept of seniority. He further pointed out that the wording of the Article refers to 'performing the functions of the Chief Justice' and not becoming the 'acting Chief Justice', which indicates that it is merely a stop-gap measure. The learned Attorney General categorically stated that the appointment of the senior-most Judge of the Supreme Court as the Chief justice is not a convention and there is no such concept of rule of seniority. He pointed out that the decision of the Appellate Division in the case of Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Justice and parliamentary Affairs and others v. Md. Idrisur Rahman, Advocate and others, 29 BLD (AD) 79 quite clearly established that there exists a positive convention of consultation with the Chief Justice before the President appoints anyone as a Judge of the Supreme Court, but there is no such consultative procedure laid down in the Constitution for the appointment of the Chief Justice. 

9. In view of the importance of the matter, we allowed the learned Attorney General to place submissions before us and since we have heard both the learned Attorney General and the petitioners at length we are in a position to pass an order on merit. 

10. Since the instant petition relates to the appointment of the Chief Justice. We will not consider any matters relating to appointment of Judges of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh. Suffice it to say that it appears from the petition that the language used by the petitioners is a reflection of the language used in the case of S.N Goswami, Advocate and another vs. Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and others, 55 DLR 332. That case related to super session of Judges when being appointed to the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh. 

11. So far as it relates to the appointment of the Chief Justice, clauses (t) and (2) of article 95 of the Constitution are relevant, which provide as follows. 
"95.(1) The Chief Justice and other Judges shall be appointed by the President. 
(2) A person shall not be qualified for appointment as a Judge unless he is a citizen of Bangladesh and-
(a) has, for not less than ten years been an advocate of the Supreme Court; or 
(b) has, for not less than ten years, held judicial office in the territory of Bangladesh; or 
(c) has such other qualifications as may be prescribed by law for appointment as a Judge of the Supreme Court." 

We may also refer to article 48(3) of the Constitution which provides as follows:

"48(3) In the exercise of all his functions, save only that of appointing the Prime Minister pursuant to clause (3) of article 56 and the Chief Justice pursuant to clause (1) of article 95, the President shall act in accordance with the advice of the Prime Minister." 

It thus appears that in the case of appointment of Judges to the Supreme Court the President is obliged to act in accordance with the advice of the Prime Minister, but in the case of appointment of the Chief Justice there is no such obligation and the President alone has the authority to appoint the Chief Justice, So far as the article 97 is concerned, the petitioner has sought to impress upon us that the senior-most Judge of the Appellate Division is mandated to perform the function of the Chief Justice in his absence and, therefore, he is the one best suited to be appointed as the next Chief Justice. However, we find that as such the provision is simply an expedient method of filling up the gap in the temporary absence of the Chief Justice, which may be caused by illness or any other cause mentioned in the article. We also find from article 97 that even the placing of the senior-most Judge of the Appellate Division to perform the function of the Chief Justice in his absence is itself a temporary measure until some other person has entered upon the office. We agree with the submissions of the learned Attorney General that this phrase "until some other person has entered upon that office" excludes the concept of seniority. In this regard it was the contention of the learned Attorney General that some other person does not necessarily mean either the senior-most Judge or indeed any other Judge. The position could be filled by any person, who qualifies to be appointed as a Judge Article 95 (2). 

On careful scrutiny, we do not find any basis for the contention of the petitioner that the appointment of Chief Justice from the senior-most Judge of the Appellate Division is a rule of seniority or a Constitutional Convention. 

12. It seems to us that both Mr. Azim and the learned Attorney General are in favour of appointment on the basis of merit, but Mr. Azim had reservations due to the fact that the near past shown appointments being made/way of supersession for purposes other than for the benefit of the judiciary, namely for political and other purposes and motives. Mr. Azim did not deny the fact that he would prefer to see appointment on merit, but he was apprehensive that the current system is not good because merit is not being taken as a criterion, rather political and other reasons are being used as criteria for the appointment. 
It seems to us, therefore, that there is some common ground, inasmuch as merit is accepted to be a good basis for appointment of the Chief justice of Bangladesh. As to who will decide on the merit, we believe the answer can be simply stated that the Constitution specifically gives the prerogative right to the President to decide as to who will be appointed as Chief Justice. In contrast to the provision of appointment of other Judges where the need is there for taking advice of the Prime Minister, there is no such provision with regard to taking any advice from any quarter in the case of appointment of the Chief Justice. No doubt the President will consider the merit of the person whom he chooses to become the Chief Justice of the country. The President is at liberty to take opinion from any quarter that the chooses in order to ascertain the merit of the candidate. 

13. We also feel that there is a need to consider the merit of any person, who may otherwise qualify to be appointed as a Judge as the Chief Justice of the country within the requirement of article 95 (2) of the Constitution. There is no authority or body of persons who may be identified as being in a position to comment on the merit of any candidate. 

14. We may mention that the mode of appointing Chief Justices and Judges in the subcontinent have been inherited from the age old conventions followed in England, but the centuries-old convention of the appointment of Judges being made by the Lord Chancellor was done away with in the year, 2006 with the promulgation of the Constitutional Reform Act, 2005. When the matter of appointment of Judges was discussed from the year 2003, Lord Faulkner, the then Secretary of State for Constitutional Affairs, asserted that it was no longer acceptable for judicial appointments to be entirely in the hands of a Government Minister (namely the Lord Chancellor) Accordingly, the British Government announced its intention to establish an independent Judicial Appointment Commission (JAC) to recommend candidates for judicial appointment on a more transparent basis. The Judicial Appointment Commission comprises 15 members, including a Chairman, who come from various vocations and professions. A Committee is selected for the purpose of selecting the Chief Justice and other Judges, and within that Committee there will always be two senior members of the judiciary and two members of the Judicial Appointment Commission. 

15. It is interesting to note that India has a system of appointing judges, other than the Chief Justice, by a collegium of judges. In Pakistan judges, other than the Chief Justice, are chosen by the Judicial Commission of Pakistan, which was set up by incorporating an amendment in their Constitution. Article 175 and 176A provide as follows: 

Amended article 175A and 176 

67. Insertion of Article 175A in the Constitution.—In the Constitution, after Article 175, the following new Article shall be inserted, namely:—

"175A. Appointment of Judges to the Supreme Court, High Courts and the Federal Shariat Court.—(l) There shall be a Judicial Commission of Pakistan, hereinafter in this Article referred to as the Commission, for appointment of Judges of the Supreme Court, High Courts and the Federal Shariat Court, as hereinafter provided. 

(2) For appointment of Judges of the Supreme Court, the Commission shall consist of 

(i) Chief Justice of Pakistan: Chairman 

(ii) two most senior Judges of the Supreme Court: Members 

(iii) a former Chief Justice or a former Judge of the Supreme Court of Pakistan to be nominated by the Chief Justice of Pakistan, in consultation with the two member Judges, for a period of two years: Member 

(iv) Federal Minister for Law and Justice: Member 

(v) Attorney General for Pakistan: Member 

(vi) a Senior Advocate of the Supreme Court of Pakistan nominated by the Pakistan Bar Council for a term of two years: Member 

(3) Notwithstanding anything contained in clause (1) or clause (2), the President shall appoint the most senior Judge of the Supreme Court as the Chief Justice of Pakistan. 

(4) The Commission may make rules regulating its procedure. 

(5) For appointment of Judges of a High Court, the Commission in clause (2) shall also include the following, namely:-
(i) Chief Justice of the High Court to which the Member appointment is being made-, 

(ii) the most senior Judge of that High Court; Member 

(iii) Provincial Minister for Law; and Member 

(iv) a senior advocate to be nominated Member by the Provincial Bar Council for a term of two years: 

Provided that for appointment of the Chief Justice of a High Court, the most senior Judge of the Court shall be substituted by a former Chief Justice or former Judge of that Court, to be nominated by the Chief Justice of Pakistan in consultation with the two member Judges of the -Commission-mentioned in clause (2): 

Provided further that if for any reason the Chief Justice of High Court is not available he shall also be substituted in the manner as provided in the foregoing proviso. 

(6) For appointment of Judges of the Islamabad High Court, the Commission in Clause (2) shall also include the following, namely: (i) Chief Justice of the Islamabad High Court; and Member, (ii) the most senior Judge of that High Court: Member. 

Provided that for initial appointment of the Judges of the Islamabad High Court, the Chief Justices of the four Provincial High Courts shall also be members of the Commission: 

Provided further that subject to the foregoing proviso, in case of appointment of Chief Justice of Islamabad High Court, the provisos to clause (5) shall mutatis mutandis, apply. 

(7) For appointment of Judges of the Federal Shariat Court, the Commission in clause (2) shall also include the Chief Justice of the Federal Shariat Court and the most senior Judge of that Court as its members: 

Provided that for appointment of Chief Justice of Federal Shariat Court, the provisos to clause (5) shall, mutatis mutandis, apply. 
(8) The Commission by majority of its total-membership shall nominate to the Parliamentary Committee one person, for each vacancy of a Judge in the Supreme Court, a High Court or the Federal Shariat Court, as the case may be; 

(9) The Parliamentary Committee, hereinafter in this Article referred to as the Committee, shall consist of the following eight members, namely: (i) four members from the Senate; and -(ii) four members from the National Assembly. 

(10) Out of the eight members of the Committee, four shall be from the Treasury Benches, two from each House and four from the Opposition Benches, two from each House. The nomination of members from the Treasury Benches shall be made by the Leader of the House and from the Opposition Benches by the Leader of the Opposition. 

(11) Secretary, Senate shall act as the Secretary of the Committee. 

(12) The Committee on receipt of a nomination from the Commission may confirm the nominee by majority of its total membership within fourteen days, failing which the nomination shall be deemed to have been confirmed: Provided that the Committee may not confirm the nomination by three-fourth majority of its total membership within the said period, in which case the Commission shall send another nomination. 

(13) The Committee shall forward the name of the nominee confirmed by it or deemed to have been confirmed to the President for appointment. 

(14) No action or decision taken by the Commission or a Committee shall be invalid or called in question only on the ground of the existence of a vacancy therein or of the absence of any member from any meeting thereof. 

(15) The Committee may make rules for regulating its procedure. 

68. Amendment of Article 177 of the Constitution.—In the Constitution, in Article 177, for clause (I) the following shall be substituted, namely: 

"(1) The Chief Justice of Pakistan and each of the other Judges of the Supreme Court shall be appointed by the President in accordance with Article 175 A 

16. Both India and Pakistan chose their Chief Justice from the senior-most Judge of the Supreme Court. It is perhaps feasible due to the system of selection of Judges of the High Courts and Supreme Court of India and Pakistan by an independent body,' which effectively results in meritorious Judges moving up the ladder ready for appointment to the position of Chief Justice. We do not have such a system in place. Here the President exercises his prerogative. Hence, merit must be discovered by the President. 

It is not for us to suggest that a Judicial Commission must be created, but we only suggest that the President may consider taking opinion, when appointing Judges or appointing the Chief Justice, from any persons whom he so chooses, including any Commission or Committee set up tinder the Constitution that he may choose for his ease of reference. We believe that in appointing the Chief Justice of the country the President would refer to all and any quarters who would advise him or assist him in choosing the right person for the post of Chief Justice and we believe that reference to any Commission made for the purpose of scrutinizing the ability of Judges to be appointed as a; Chief Justice would lead to transparency in the system of appointment. Allegations of politicising appointments are abundant, as can be seen from the judgment of the High Court Division in Md. Idrisur Rahman and others, V The Secretary, Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs, 29 BLD 32. This niggling complaint pervades through the different strata of our society. It is our view that possibilities of any appointments being made, on political -considerations would be minimised if the selection was to be made by an independent constitutional body and to be decided finally by the President. 

17. With regard to the petitioners' claim that reasons must be assigned for supersession, since we do not accept that there is any rule of appointing from the senior-most Judges, no question of assigning reasons could arise. Moreover, we agree with the learned Attorney General that giving reasons would only stigmatize the Hon'ble Judges who are superseded. 

18. With the above observations, we dispose, of the application without issuing any Rule. 

19. The learned advocate makes an oral application that a certificate may be issued under article 103(2)(a) of the Constitution since, according to his submission, the matter involves a substantial, question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution. However, we have already expressed our view that the provision of the Constitution with regard to the appointment of the Chief Justice is clear and does not call for any interpretation. Hence, the application is rejected. 

End.
